query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a controlled amount of tungsten carbide (WC) particles into the high-entropy alloy (HEA) matrix will reduce both the coefficient of friction and the wear rate of self‐lubricating moving components over a wide temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: An unreinforced HEA with a single-phase FCC solid solution structure that exhibits higher friction and wear under sliding conditions.
generation.intervention: Introduce a dispersed phase of WC particles (optimally around 20-25% by volume) into the HEA using a process such as spark plasma sintering (SPS) to form a WC–HEA composite.
generation.conditions: Sliding contact tests performed over a service-temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C under controlled load and speed conditions, using a ceramic counterface.
generation.structural_mediator: The WC particles promote the formation of secondary carbide phases (e.g., Cr-rich carbides and Co3W3C) within a modified microstructure that enhances hardness and provides nucleation sites for protective oxide layers.
generation.mechanism: The intervention reduces friction and wear by: (1) increasing the composite’s overall hardness through second-phase strengthening, (2) modifying the wear mechanism from primarily adhesive to a more controlled abrasive mode, and (3) facilitating the formation of a lubricious, sacrificial oxide film during sliding.
generation.predicted_outcome: The WC–HEA composite is expected to show a significant reduction in both the coefficient of friction (approximately 20-25% lower than the untreated HEA) and the wear rate across the full temperature range compared to the baseline material.
generation.baseline: The untreated HEA, which exhibits higher friction and increased wear due to adhesive and abrasive wear mechanisms under similar testing conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected to diminish if the WC content exceeds approximately 30%, as excessive carbide formation may compromise interfacial bonding and lubrication efficacy; additionally, the optimal performance is contingent on maintaining controlled processing conditions and specific sliding parameters.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal WC content and quantitative performance improvements remain uncertain, as well as potential influences of sliding speed, load variations, and long-term microstructural stability under cyclic thermal conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of untreated HEA and one set of WC–HEA composite (with ~20-25% WC by volume) via SPS processing. Subject both sets to identical sliding wear tests over a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C using a tribometer with a ceramic counterface, maintaining constant load and sliding speed. Conduct parallel microstructural analyses.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (COF) monitored during sliding at each temperature
Wear volume loss measured after a fixed sliding distance
Microstructural characterization (using SEM and EDS) of wear tracks and oxide layer formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the WC–HEA composite does not exhibit at least a 20% reduction in both COF and wear rate compared to the untreated HEA across the temperature range, or if the expected secondary carbide phases and protective oxide layers are not observed, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Besides, the variations of the coefficient of friction (COF) of the tested CCAs with increasing temperature from RT to 800 °C are similar to the variations of their wear rates (Fig. S6). Specifically, the COF of the Ni3X is 0.54 at RT, increasing to about 0.64 between 400 °C and 600 °C, and then decreasing to 0.49 at 800 °C. For NiX, its COF is around 0.25 at RT, increasing to 0.52 at 400 °C, whereas it decreases to 0.43 and 0.36 at 600 °C and 800 °C, respectively. Figure 3B to E and Fig. S7 show the scanning electron microscope (SEM) images and 3-dimensional (3D) morphologies of the worn tracks for the NiX and Ni3X at a temperature range from RT to 800 °C. The results suggest that the wear mechanism of both CCAs between RT and 400 °C is primarily abrasive wear, while their wear between 600 °C and 800 °C is characterized by oxidative and adhesive wear. At RT, Ni3X produces a rough worn surface covered with grooved scratches and wear debris as in conventional alloys (Fig. 3B), resulting from strain localization initiated during the groove multiplication process [,]. EDS analysis (Table S2) indicates that the wear debris has a higher oxygen concentration compared to the worn surface.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.3. The Effect of WC Content on Properties of Composites
cited_evidence.text: The strengthening mechanisms of WC particle-reinforced HEA matrix composites mainly include the second phase strengthening of the hard phase itself, the dislocation strengthening introduced by the difference in thermal expansion coefficients between the hard phase and the matrix, the fine grain strengthening of the matrix grains by the hard phase during the ball milling process, and solid solution strengthening caused by diffusion of W and C atoms [,].

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.3. The Effect of WC Content on Properties of Composites
cited_evidence.text: WC particles have high hardness, good wear resistance, strong resistance to deformation during friction, and are less prone to plastic deformation, resulting in increased friction resistance and stronger wear resistance of the composites. With the increase of WC content, the wear mechanism of HEA matrix composites changes from adhesive wear to abrasive wear, and the formation of second phases such as Cr-rich and Co3W3C carbides in the composites also reduces the wear volume, which is beneficial to the improvement of wear resistance of HEA matrix. When the WC content increases to 30%, the WC content is too much, resulting in an excessive amount of the Cr-rich phase being generated in the composite, leading to more prominent interface problems, affecting the bonding between the hard phase and the matrix, resulting in a poor overall lubrication effect and increased friction coefficient of the composite. However, overall, compared with the Cr-rich phase, the distribution of WC particles in the 30 WC–HEA sample is more dispersed, and the effect of WC is more prominent. In this work, WC-FeCoCrNi composites were prepared by the SPS process. The effects of WC content on the microstructure, mechanical properties, and wear resistance of WC–HEA composites were studied. The main conclusions are as follows: A single-phase FCC solid solution structure was formed after SPS sintering of the HEA pure matrix powder, which did not appear before sintering, indicating that SPS is helpful for HEA to complete alloying. The sintered WC–HEA composite is mainly composed of an FCC matrix phase (Ni, Fe) and carbide phases (Cr7C3, Co3W3C, WC, etc.). With the increase of WC content, the distribution of WC is dispersed, and the content of Cr7C3 and Co3W3C increases gradually. Some needle-like Cr-rich phases in the FCC matrix coarsen into flakes. Although the addition of WC reduces the densification of the composite to a certain extent, it significantly improves the hardness and compressive yield strength of the matrix. The microhardness of the 30 WC–HEA composite is the highest, at 459.2 HV, which is 71.2% higher than that of the pure matrix material.
